criterion_notes.c1: The paper discusses community water, sanitation, and hygiene (WASH) development and service provision in Ghana, including WaterAid Ghana's community water and sanitation programming.
criterion_notes.c2: Plain reading vs. narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading: Under the plain broad wording of Criterion 2, the paper touches on institutional and governance themes—specifically international/local NGO ('neo-comprador') aid relationships, donor governance, traditional authorities, and community Water and Sanitation Management Teams—so it passes the broad literal phrasing of Criterion 2. Under the narrow 2026-10-13 clarification, however, it fails Criterion 2 ('no'): its focus is an endogenous development (ED) cultural/epistemological approach to NGO WASH project delivery, community sensitisation, and sanitation/hygiene behaviour change alongside a macro-critique of Western aid and philanthrocapitalism, rather than any rule-type legal, administrative, or regulatory mechanism directly governing service access (such as eligibility rules, tenure/documentation requirements, tariffs, enforcement, or utility regulation). Note that plain_criterion2_decision remains 'exclude' because the paper also fails Criterion 3 (no empirical evidence/methods).
criterion_notes.c3: Fails Criterion 3: the article is a theoretical critique of Western neoliberal development/INGOs combined with a first-person practitioner reflection by a WaterAid Ghana leader on introducing endogenous development (ED) into WASH programming. It reports no empirical research design, data collection methods, sampling strategy, or systematic primary data analysis, offering only brief programmatic anecdotes and quotes from an unpublished internal mid-term review.
criterion_notes.c4: Unclear / anecdotal only: mostly discusses cultural worldviews, participation, and hygiene/sanitation behaviour change, with only passing anecdotal mention of sinking a borehole near a sacred river and a community using local resources to extend the reach of a water point, without systematic measurement of service access outcomes.
criterion_notes.c5: Fails Criterion 5: lacks an identifiable empirical study design, defined study sample, and systematically operationalised exposure and access outcome.
criterion_notes.c6: Published in English (abstracts in English, French, and Spanish; full text in English).

evidence_quotes.quote: This article examines it to determine its value in creating sustainable, culturally-relevant solutions to WASH issues in Africa, in this case in Ghana.
The ED approach requires knowledge of the meanings and worldview understandings of WASH issues found within a community.

Using a water, sanitation, and hygiene (WASH) sector case study from Ghana, the article theorises Africa’s WASH development within the context of globalisation and the politics of knowledge production on Africa.

Viewing development as a cultural process, I have used my leadership position within the INGO WaterAid’s country programme in Ghana to promote ED as a means to tackle the poor WASH situation (especially sanitation).
The ED project results include: community resources used to extend the reach of the water point by the community

raw_response.exposure: Endogenous development (ED) praxis centring African indigenous culture, worldviews, and traditional community structures in NGO WASH project delivery and sanitation/hygiene behaviour change
raw_response.outcome: Anecdotal programme highlights regarding cultural sensitisation, sanitation/hygiene behaviour change, borehole siting, reconstituting a Water and Sanitation Management Team, and extending a community water point (not systematically measured)
raw_response.population_and_sample: Communities participating in WaterAid Ghana's AACES endogenous development programme (including an illustrative vignette of Okrakwadwo community, Eastern Region, population 1,338); no research sampling frame reported
raw_response.rationale: Excluded as E05 (No empirical evidence), and also fails the narrow 2026-10-13 Criterion 2 scope. The article is a theoretical/conceptual essay critiquing Western aid, 'neo-comprador' NGOs, and philanthrocapitalism paired with first-person practitioner reflections on introducing endogenous development (indigenous cultural worldviews and hygiene/sanitation behaviour change) into WaterAid Ghana's WASH programming. It presents no empirical research methodology, sampling, or systematic primary data analysis, and examines NGO cultural/behavioural project delivery rather than a rule-type legal, administrative, or regulatory mechanism governing service access. Even under the plain wording of Criterion 2, it remains excluded for lack of empirical methods and study design.
raw_response.study_design: Theoretical essay and practitioner programme reflection (non-empirical)
